text: How does a hydraulic press crush almost anything? Your arm pushes. The oil multiplies.
Here's a twenty-ton shop press, taken apart: frame, hand pump, oil reservoir, and one big cylinder.
Lift the handle: a small piston sucks in oil through a check valve. Push down: it's forced out through a second one.
It can't flow back, so every stroke stacks more oil on the big piston: the ram.
Pascal's law: squeeze a trapped liquid, and the pressure is equal everywhere. Force is pressure times area.
Pump piston: seven sixteenths of an inch wide. Ram: two and a quarter. Twenty-six times the area.
The handle turns a ninety-pound pull into fifteen hundred pounds on the small piston: ten thousand P S I. On the ram, forty thousand pounds. Twenty tons.
The catch? Each stroke moves the ram about a millimeter. You trade distance for force.
A gauge reads the pressure. A release valve lets the oil drain back.
And a soda can? It buckles at about two hundred pounds. Half a percent of this press.
What should we take apart next?
Congrats! You've discovered the hydraulic press.
